title: St. Valentines Day

jokes.text: Good morning, Regular Person Lemon.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Good morning, Dr. Baird' in a normal, professional way.
jokes.punchline: Drew mirrors the greeting but replaces her name with 'Regular Person Lemon,' an absurd hierarchical title that implies she is beneath him by default.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly characterizes Drew's oblivious, classifying handsomeness — he genuinely doesn't mean it as an insult, which makes it funnier. The parallel structure (Dr. Baird / Regular Person Lemon) is tight and economical. High character integration because only this specific character archetype could deliver it with earnest sincerity.

jokes.text: Saturday is Valentine's Day? Norts!
jokes.setup: Liz agrees to a Saturday date and is relieved it doesn't have to be weird.
jokes.punchline: She discovers Saturday IS Valentine's Day and exclaims 'Norts!' — a made-up, childish expletive perfectly capturing her arrested-development energy.
jokes.explanation: 'Norts!' is an invented expletive that is pure Liz Lemon — childish, endearing, and completely specific to her. The word itself is the joke. It's maximally economical (one word does everything), highly quotable, and perfectly character-integrated. Scores high because the invented word does so much comedic work so efficiently.

jokes.text: You sound so sexy when you say that. Say it again.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Norts!' in exasperation about Valentine's Day.
jokes.punchline: Drew finds her childish made-up word arousing and asks her to repeat it — simultaneously mocking her and showing his shallow, looks-over-everything personality.
jokes.explanation: Immediate callback that recontextualizes 'Norts' as sexy, which is absurd. Works as character comedy for Drew — he's attracted to her despite (or because of) her weirdness, which is funny because it implies he's not actually listening to the words.

jokes.text: The McFlurry metaphor — 'Some would say that describes us. Who would say such a crazy thing?' / 'We are us. The world's greatest dessert.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Elisa are sharing a McFlurry and Jack draws a romantic metaphor between the dessert's complementary flavors and their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Elisa deflects the sentimentality with 'Who would say such a crazy thing?' then Jack doubles down with the hilariously pompous 'We are us. The world's greatest dessert.' — self-aggrandizement disguised as romance.
jokes.explanation: Jack Donaghy's narcissism expressing itself through romance is well-worn but well-executed here. 'We are us. The world's greatest dessert' is delightfully pompous. The joke is in the gap between the grandiosity and the fact that they're eating McDonald's.

jokes.text: Actually, the world's greatest dessert is served in a restaurant right here in New York called Plunder. It costs $1,000.
jokes.setup: Jack has just called their McFlurry-based relationship 'the world's greatest dessert.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to inform her that actually the world's greatest dessert is a $1,000 dish at an elite restaurant — undercutting his own romantic metaphor with plutocratic one-upmanship.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant self-contradiction — Jack sincerely means both things simultaneously. The callback to his own romantic statement to introduce a $1,000 dessert is perfect Jack Donaghy character comedy. Only this specific character archetype (the plutocrat who genuinely can't separate commerce from romance) could deliver this with straight-faced authenticity.

jokes.text: Don't tell me you're one of those convenient Catholics that only goes to church every Sunday.
jokes.setup: Elisa wants to go to church on Valentine's Day. Jack implies this is inconvenient and overly devout.
jokes.punchline: Jack's definition of a 'convenient Catholic' is someone who only goes 'every Sunday' — revealing that even weekly church attendance is, to him, extreme religiosity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is perfectly inverted — 'convenient Catholic' is a real phrase meaning someone who only follows religion when convenient, but Jack redefines it to mean someone who goes EVERY Sunday, which reveals his total alienation from faith. The structure is elegant, the economy is perfect, and it's extremely quotable. Only Jack Donaghy could deliver this with complete sincerity.

jokes.text: Do I? I wouldn't have this job if it weren't for the mouth on my back.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks Kenneth if he knows that the company makes an effort to hire the disabled.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth casually reveals he has a mouth on his back, which is why he qualifies as disabled — delivered with complete earnestness as if this is a normal thing.
jokes.explanation: Pure 30 Rock absurdism at its finest. 'The mouth on my back' is a grotesque, surreal detail dropped with zero fanfare by Kenneth, who treats it as completely unremarkable. The contrast between the mundane delivery and the horrifying image is the entire joke. It never gets explained or revisited, which is the correct choice. High originality — this specific image is genuinely surprising and strange.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm supposed to supervise some blind chick they hired to edit the reruns. But three of the dancers just found out they're all dating the same guy, so I'm going to go watch that.
jokes.setup: Tracy has a work responsibility — supervising a newly hired blind editor.
jokes.punchline: He immediately abandons the responsibility to watch reality-show-style drama unfold among dancers — and explains this to Kenneth as if it's a perfectly reasonable professional decision.
jokes.explanation: Efficiently characterizes Tracy's chaos and amorality. The specificity of 'three of the dancers just found out they're all dating the same guy' grounds the absurdity in a believable TRL-era NBC backstage reality. Tracy's complete lack of guilt is the joke.

jokes.text: All my friends warned me about the big city. But, look. Right away, I meet a gentleman.
jokes.setup: Jennifer, a blind woman new to NYC, is relieved to meet Kenneth immediately after arriving.
jokes.punchline: The irony is that she can't see Kenneth — who is, by the show's framing, a naive, possibly supernatural oddity — and takes his helpfulness as evidence the city is safe. The joke is that her trust is misplaced not because the city is dangerous, but because Kenneth is bizarre.
jokes.explanation: Functional irony setup — the audience knows more than Jennifer does, and the joke relies on that dramatic irony. Not particularly original but well-placed as setup for the Kenneth/Jennifer storyline.

jokes.text: Is everything okay? Because now, I smell burnt plastic.
jokes.setup: Jennifer has just been helped by Kenneth and seems reassured. Something has clearly gone wrong in the background (implied visual gag).
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's blindness means she can only detect the disaster through smell — 'burnt plastic' — which is both a reaction beat to an unseen physical comedy moment and a character-specific way of experiencing the world.
jokes.explanation: Smart use of Jennifer's blindness as a comedic device — her perceiving the world differently (through smell rather than sight) is both funny and economical. The joke implies a physical comedy disaster that we presumably see but the transcript only hints at. 'Burnt plastic' is a funny specific choice of smell.

jokes.text: What is this, a green card thing? ... Closet case? ... Slut buster? ... Bundy-esque serial killer?
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to diagnose why a handsome man would pursue a first date on Valentine's Day with Liz.
jokes.punchline: His list of possible explanations escalates from plausible (green card) to absurd (Bundy-esque serial killer), with 'Slut buster' as the absurdist peak in the middle — and Liz neutrally responding to each one.
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock list comedy — the rapid-fire escalation through possible reasons why Drew would date Liz is both a joke about her self-image and a great showcase for Jack's diagnostic, transactional worldview. 'Slut buster' is the unexpected peak. Liz's deadpan 'Not a ball player' response to 'Slut buster' is an excellent secondary punchline. The list structure is tight and the escalation is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: people in love and rings hidden in pastries... Ugh.
jokes.setup: Jack is advising Liz not to go to a restaurant on Valentine's Day because it will be full of romantic clichés.
jokes.punchline: Liz's disgusted 'Ugh' at the mention of 'rings hidden in pastries' — romantic proposals — is a perfect reaction beat that confirms her anti-romance stance while also getting a laugh from the audience who expected her to want that.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Liz's repulsion at romance is well-established and this confirms it efficiently. Not a stand-out joke but does character work in one sound.

jokes.text: Nice? You mean, like, stew? / I certainly do not mean stew.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz to cook her date 'a nice meal at home.'
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate interpretation of 'nice meal' is stew — a deliberately unglamorous, unflattering choice that perfectly captures her culinary and romantic blind spots.
jokes.explanation: Stew is the perfect comedic choice — it's the least romantic food imaginable. Jack's horrified 'I certainly do not mean stew' sells it further. The exchange is tight and funny, establishing that Liz will, of course, make stew — which pays off later in the episode.

jokes.text: If I had those knockers, I'd be thanking God, too.
jokes.setup: Elisa wants to go to church. Jack dismisses religion but acknowledges her devotion.
jokes.punchline: Jack attributes Elisa's Catholicism entirely to gratitude for her physical assets — reducing genuine faith to vanity, which is both offensive and perfectly in-character for Jack.
jokes.explanation: Very Jack — he can't conceive of religion as anything but transactional or vain. The specific word 'knockers' adds a period flavor that makes it funnier. Solid character integration.

jokes.text: Tahitian vanilla bean ice cream in a pool of cognac drizzled in the world's most expensive chocolate — Amedei Porceleana — covered with shaved white, black and clear truffles and topped with edible 25-karat gold leaf.
jokes.setup: Jack describes the 'Lovers' Delight' dessert at Plunder.
jokes.punchline: The joke is the escalating extravagance of the description — each ingredient more expensive and absurd than the last, culminating in 'edible 25-karat gold leaf,' delivered with utter sincerity by Jack.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Jack's complete earnestness — he's not showing off, he genuinely believes this is reasonable. The escalation of luxury ingredients works because each one is slightly more absurd. 'Edible 25-karat gold leaf' is the correct landing point.

jokes.text: Can you imagine anything better? / I don't know. Have you ever put a donut in the microwave?
jokes.setup: Jack has just finished describing an elaborate $1,000 gourmet dessert and asks if anything could top it.
jokes.punchline: Liz genuinely considers the question and offers 'a donut in the microwave' as a sincere rival to 25-karat gold ice cream — which perfectly encapsulates the Jack/Liz dynamic and Liz's character.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Jack's elaborate, rapturous description of a $1,000 dessert sets up the expectation of either agreement or an equally sophisticated counter. Instead, Liz offers a microwaved donut — delivered with genuine consideration ('I don't know') as if it's a legitimately close call. The 'I don't know' is crucial — it means she's actually weighing the options. Maximum character integration (only Liz Lemon could say this), perfect economy, completely earned. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: NBC? Blah, blah, blah. Thank you. / Ken, you need to snap out of it and ask out that sexy Ms. Magoo.
jokes.setup: Tracy is dismissing an NBC phone call mid-sentence.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's summary of an entire NBC communication as 'blah, blah, blah' is a great bit of institutional contempt, followed immediately by his use of 'sexy Ms. Magoo' as a term of affection for a blind woman.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes compacted into one beat. 'Blah, blah, blah. Thank you.' as a complete phone call summary is classic Tracy. 'Sexy Ms. Magoo' is an inspired nickname — Mr. Magoo was famously blind, so it's appropriate and affectionate in Tracy's tactless way.

jokes.text: I saw it when I met Angie. I saw it the first time Dotcom laid eyes on Grizz's fiancee.
jokes.setup: Tracy claims he knows love at first sight, citing examples.
jokes.punchline: He uses 'Dotcom laying eyes on Grizz's fiancee' as an example of love at first sight — which implies ongoing infidelity/betrayal within his entourage, delivered as if it's a sweet romantic memory.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark joke buried in apparent sweetness. Tracy is innocently describing what is clearly an ongoing affair/betrayal between his entourage members — and he cites it as an example of beautiful love. The casual delivery of what would be a devastating interpersonal bomb is the whole joke. Very Tracy.

jokes.text: There is something about Jennifer that just makes me all carsick inside.
jokes.setup: Tracy has told Kenneth to pursue Jennifer. Kenneth tries to articulate his feelings.
jokes.punchline: 'Carsick inside' as a description of romantic feelings — Kenneth's folksy, inadvertently grotesque way of describing butterflies/love is both characterful and funny.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's folksy Kentucky idiom replacing normal romantic vocabulary is a staple of his character done well here. 'Carsick inside' is specific enough to be surprising but also logically follows his general communication style. High character integration.

jokes.text: Oh! It's you again. I can tell.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has apparently encountered Jennifer again. She recognizes him.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's 'I can tell' — implying she recognizes Kenneth by smell/sound/aura rather than sight — is a gentle joke about blindness that works because it raises the question of HOW she can tell, which is left enticingly vague.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sweet. The ambiguity of 'I can tell' — is it his voice? His smell? His aura? — is funnier than any explanation would be.

jokes.text: Well, cotton and fiddles.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is about to approach Jennifer and is delighted/flustered.
jokes.punchline: 'Cotton and fiddles' as a folksy exclamation replaces a normal reaction — it's pure Kenneth, a nonsensical phrase that sounds like it means something but is just vague rural Americana.
jokes.explanation: Pure Kenneth absurdism. 'Cotton and fiddles' sounds like it could be an idiom but isn't one — it's two rural nouns combined into a pseudo-exclamation. High character integration and economy. The phrase sticks in the mind.

jokes.text: You may call me Kenneth the page because that is who I am.
jokes.setup: Kenneth introduces himself to Jennifer.
jokes.punchline: The tautological explanation 'because that is who I am' after stating his name and title — as if the explanation were necessary — is classic Kenneth literalism.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's childlike sincerity expressed through logical tautology. Saying 'because that is who I am' adds nothing informational but reveals everything about his character — he explains himself as if identity requires justification.

jokes.text: Yes, indeedy corncobs?
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Jennifer out.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer responds with 'Yes, indeedy corncobs?' — a folksy affirmative that matches Kenneth's register but is entirely her own invention, suggesting she's from a similar background or just equally eccentric.
jokes.explanation: The joke works by pairing Kenneth's absurdist folksy register with Jennifer matching it — suggesting they're cosmically compatible in their rural eccentricity. 'Corncobs' as a filler noun is a funny specific choice.

jokes.text: ...except for looking at that eclipse.
jokes.setup: Jennifer says her instincts have never let her down.
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies this with 'except for looking at that eclipse' — implying that her blindness was self-inflicted by staring at an eclipse, delivered as a casual aside.
jokes.explanation: Absolutely brilliant. The joke earns its high scores because it is genuinely unexpected — we don't expect the show to address how Jennifer became blind, and when it does, the answer is both absurd and dark. 'Except for looking at that eclipse' as a throwaway qualifier is structurally perfect — she buries the devastating self-indictment inside a positive statement. The economy is flawless: six words reveal that she blinded herself through poor judgment, which is both funny and darkly sad. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: It's a Valentine's date-li-doo!
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Jennifer have agreed to go on a date.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth celebrates by saying 'date-li-doo' — an invented compound word combining 'date' with a nonsense suffix, expressing joy in his uniquely childlike way.
jokes.explanation: Another Kenneth invented compound word/phrase that works entirely through character specificity. 'Date-li-doo' is the kind of word only he would coin.

jokes.text: That was really good stew. / Thank you. It's my own recipe where I use cheddar cheese instead of water.
jokes.setup: Drew compliments Liz's stew (she made stew, despite Jack's warning).
jokes.punchline: Liz explains her stew recipe uses 'cheddar cheese instead of water' — an absurd substitution that raises many questions about the physics of this stew and confirms she has no culinary instincts.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the earlier stew setup. The callback is earned and the punchline is genuinely inspired — 'cheddar cheese instead of water' is specific, disgusting, and completely plausible as a Liz Lemon innovation. The fact that Drew calls it 'really good' is a secondary joke (he's being polite or is too handsome to know better). One of the episode's stronger jokes due to the combination of callback satisfaction and the specific absurdity of the recipe.

jokes.text: Yeah, you still have that rotting jack-o-lantern in the hallway, so I feel like you don't have a great sense of what month it is.
jokes.setup: Liz has explained she didn't realize it was Valentine's Day when she invited Drew over.
jokes.punchline: Drew points out the rotting Halloween pumpkin still in her hallway as evidence that she's fundamentally out of sync with the calendar — specific, visual, and perfectly targeted at Liz.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke with excellent visual grounding. The jack-o-lantern is a perfectly specific detail that tells us everything about Liz's domestic life. Drew's delivery as a calm, reasonable observation (not a criticism) makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Well, it's just gotten so small that I kind of want to see if it disappears.
jokes.setup: Drew has pointed out her rotting jack-o-lantern.
jokes.punchline: Liz explains she's keeping it to run a decomposition experiment — she wants to 'see if it disappears' — which is a completely Liz-like rationalization for laziness as curiosity.
jokes.explanation: Liz's self-justification of laziness as scientific inquiry is funny and very character-specific. 'I kind of want to see if it disappears' is a perfect Liz rationalization.

jokes.text: I feel like I should do the right thing here and tell you that your breast has fallen out of your blouse and I can see all of it.
jokes.setup: Liz is sharing an 'interesting' story about being born on the border of Maryland and Pennsylvania.
jokes.punchline: Drew interrupts with clinical detachment to inform her of a wardrobe malfunction — the formality of 'I feel like I should do the right thing here' followed by the specificity of 'I can see all of it' is both awkward and hilarious.
jokes.explanation: Well-executed cringe comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: the interruption of Liz's boring story, Drew's physician-like detachment in how he delivers the news, and the specificity of 'I can see all of it.' The formality of 'I feel like I should do the right thing here' before a wardrobe malfunction announcement is very funny.

jokes.text: Okay. Well, I guess we just... jumped ahead to date four. / It's not the good one, either.
jokes.setup: Liz's breast has been exposed on their first date.
jokes.punchline: Liz reframes the moment as 'date four' (implying dates have standard physical progression), then Drew immediately clarifies it's 'not the good one' — implying there's a better date (date five? six?) that involves more.
jokes.explanation: Excellent two-part joke. Liz's 'date four' reframe is already clever — it defuses embarrassment by gamifying the situation. But Drew's 'It's not the good one, either' is the perfect second beat: it's understated, it implies there's a better date further down the line, and it's deadpan. The economy is exceptional — 'It's not the good one, either' does enormous work in very few words. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jonathan... our Jonathan, who art in the office / hallowed be my reservation. / If you are able... / hold my table / at Plunder / as we will not be there by seven. / Have them delay our heavenly dessert / and forgive us our lateness...
jokes.setup: Jack is calling his assistant Jonathan to hold his restaurant reservation.
jokes.punchline: Jack delivers the message as a parody of the Lord's Prayer, treating his restaurant reservation as a sacred covenant and his assistant as God — the structural parallel is meticulous and the substitutions are perfectly chosen.
jokes.explanation: A sustained parody of the Lord's Prayer as a restaurant voicemail is a premium 30 Rock joke. Each line maps precisely to the prayer ('hallowed be my reservation,' 'forgive us our lateness'), and it contextualizes Jack's faith-in-capitalism perfectly given the episode's religion theme. 'Heavenly dessert' as a substitute for 'daily bread' is brilliant. High structure, high character integration — this is the kind of joke that takes genuine craft to write.

jokes.text: Oh, cheese stew. What was I thinking?
jokes.setup: Liz is in the middle of her date and apparently realizes her cheese-stew gambit was a mistake.
jokes.punchline: The self-recrimination 'What was I thinking?' applied to a stew she made by replacing water with cheddar cheese — a callback to the earlier recipe joke.
jokes.explanation: A light callback that works mostly as a brief beat of Liz's self-awareness. Functional but not particularly strong on its own.

jokes.text: I think your brownies are burning. You want me to take them out? / Oh, yes, please, um, but whatever you do don't open that kitchen window. / No! / Oh! Too soon!
jokes.setup: Liz has burning brownies in the kitchen and urgently tells Drew not to open the kitchen window.
jokes.punchline: Drew opens the window anyway ('No!'), causing a chain reaction disaster ('Oh! Too soon!') — the urgency of the warning makes the inevitable violation funnier, and 'Too soon!' implies something irreversible has happened.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation — the more specifically you warn someone not to do something, the more inevitable and funny it is when they do it. 'Too soon!' is the right amount of vague about what exactly happened.

jokes.text: So, we skipped from date four to date... 20. / No, date never! I would never let that happen. / Liz, it's okay. I'm a doctor. I've seen much worse. / Really? / I'm just kidding. That was pretty bad.
jokes.setup: Something bad has happened due to the window/brownie incident — apparently a significant wardrobe or physical mishap.
jokes.punchline: Drew claims as a doctor he's 'seen much worse,' Liz is briefly reassured, then Drew admits 'I'm just kidding. That was pretty bad.' — the reversal is perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: The date-numbering callback plus the doctor's reversal lands well. 'I'm just kidding. That was pretty bad.' is an excellent punchline because it's the honest thing a doctor might think but never say — Drew's bluntness (itself a running joke) surfaces here at Liz's expense. The structure (reassurance → reversal) is clean.

jokes.text: Hold on, hold on. I'm sorry. I have to get this. Hello? Mandy... / Mandy? Is that, like, a guy friend, like Mandy Patinkin?
jokes.setup: Drew gets a phone call mid-date and Liz hears the name 'Mandy.'
jokes.punchline: Liz's anxious rationalization — 'Is that, like, a guy friend, like Mandy Patinkin?' — reveals her insecurity while also being a funny celebrity name-drop that actually works because Mandy Patinkin is a real, specific person.
jokes.explanation: Mandy Patinkin is a great specific celebrity to name-drop because he's famous enough to be recognizable but not so obvious a choice. The joke is in Liz's obvious anxiety beneath the casual question. Good character integration.

jokes.text: You will see her. You will say she's cute. But let me just say that she is... complicated.
jokes.setup: Drew warns Liz about his daughter before she arrives.
jokes.punchline: The euphemistic 'complicated' after the specific instruction to call her 'cute' suggests a child who is genuinely difficult — which pays off immediately.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Bethany jokes. 'Complicated' is doing a lot of work here, and the instruction 'you will say she's cute' is funnier than it appears — Drew has clearly run this script before. Functional.

jokes.text: Mom's keying your car.
jokes.setup: Drew opens the door to his daughter Bethany for the first time on the date.
jokes.punchline: Bethany's opening line — completely deadpan — is that her mother is currently vandalizing Drew's car outside. No greeting, no introduction, just immediate devastating news delivered casually.
jokes.explanation: One of the best single-line jokes in the episode. 'Mom's keying your car' as a child's opening greeting — replacing 'hi' with devastating news, delivered with complete deadpan — is perfectly constructed. The economy is exceptional (four words communicate an entire domestic disaster and a child's numbed relationship with parental warfare). High quotability, enormous impact as a room joke.

jokes.text: Why don't you ever trust me? / Because, honey, you keep setting fire to things.
jokes.setup: Drew takes Bethany's purse. She protests.
jokes.punchline: Drew's explanation — 'Because, honey, you keep setting fire to things' — reveals Bethany is a child arsonist. Delivered with parental tenderness despite describing something terrifying.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. 'You keep setting fire to things' is horrifying information delivered in a gentle, loving parental tone — the tonal contrast is the joke. It also explains why the purse confiscation is necessary (she presumably has a lighter). The 'honey' softener makes it funnier. High quotability.

jokes.text: And now, a prayer for the pregnant members of our congregation: Anita Alvarez, Anna Alvarez, Annabelle Alvarez...
jokes.setup: We're in a Catholic church with Jack and Elisa. A priest begins reading a list of pregnant congregants.
jokes.punchline: The list is all Alvarezes — suggesting a single family or community of prolific fertility — and continues long enough that it becomes a joke about both Catholic birth rates and the endless nature of Catholic ritual.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the list's length and uniformity. All Alvarezes suggests either a very large family or a specific community pattern, and the escalating 'Anita, Anna, Annabelle' with presumably more to come functions as an escalation joke about Catholic fertility and church endurance.

jokes.text: Honey, this is a Catholic church. We'll be here until morning.
jokes.setup: The priest is reading a long list of pregnant congregants.
jokes.punchline: Jack — who doesn't want to be at church — resignedly tells Elisa they'll be there until morning, treating Catholic church length as a well-known fact to be managed.
jokes.explanation: Solid observational joke about Catholic Mass length. Jack's resigned delivery makes it funnier — it's not a complaint, it's a fact he's accepted. Works but not particularly original.

jokes.text: Okay, here's how this is going to go. We're going to sit here in silence for about three minutes. Then, I'm going to take my girlfriend to Plunder where the Pope himself could not get a table. / You sound troubled, my son. / Can it, Father. That was a nice try, though.
jokes.setup: Jack is in the confession booth, clearly not intending to confess.
jokes.punchline: Jack lays out his non-confession plan ('sit here in silence for three minutes') then when the priest attempts a pastoral opening, Jack dismisses him with 'Can it, Father. That was a nice try, though.' — treating the priest like an underperforming sales associate.
jokes.explanation: 'Can it, Father. That was a nice try, though.' is an excellent line — 'Can it' is a perfectly Jack register of dismissal, and 'That was a nice try, though' converts the priest's genuine pastoral concern into a failed sales pitch. 'Where the Pope himself could not get a table' is also a great boast. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Man, can you believe we're working on Valentine's night? My fiancee is gonna be upset. Not to worry, I sent her flowers and a beautiful card. You're the best. Don't you have faith?
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Jennifer are apparently working (at the restaurant) on Valentine's night.
jokes.punchline: The exchange works as a light character beat — Kenneth being considerate of his fiancée while also complimenting Jennifer, with Jennifer noting 'You're the best' — but the joke is that they're on a date and yet Kenneth frames it as work.
jokes.explanation: This section is slightly confusing without full scene context — it seems to be Tracy speaking about his fiancée, not Kenneth. Weaker material — functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: I have faith... in things I can see and buy and deregulate. Capitalism is my religion.
jokes.setup: Elisa asks if Jack has faith.
jokes.punchline: 'I have faith in things I can see and buy and deregulate. Capitalism is my religion.' — Jack's credo, delivered with complete sincerity, reducing metaphysical faith to market mechanics.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Jack Donaghy character lines in the episode. 'Capitalism is my religion' is a perfectly compact statement of his worldview, but the setup — 'things I can see and buy and deregulate' — is what elevates it. 'Deregulate' is the unexpected third item in the list that confirms his faith is specifically financial/political. Highly quotable, maximum character integration, excellent economy.

jokes.text: You want to have an intellectual argument? Fine. But I should warn you I went to Princeton. / I went to Harvard Divinity School. / You Crimson guys never miss a chance, do you?
jokes.setup: Jack threatens an intellectual argument using Princeton as his credential.
jokes.punchline: The priest one-ups him with Harvard Divinity School, and Jack's response — 'You Crimson guys never miss a chance, do you?' — pivots from theology to Ivy League rivalry, treating the school affiliation as more significant than the argument itself.
jokes.explanation: Sharp. Jack's pivot from faith debate to Ivy League rivalry is perfect character comedy — it reveals that institutional prestige competition is more instinctive to him than theological argument. 'You Crimson guys never miss a chance' positions Harvard pride as a kind of rival religion, which ties into the episode's theme.

jokes.text: I hit my mother with a car... possibly by accident.
jokes.setup: Jack is confessing his sins to the priest.
jokes.punchline: 'Possibly by accident' — the qualifier on hitting his mother with a car suggests genuine ambiguity about whether it was intentional, delivered as casually as the other sins.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Possibly by accident' is a masterpiece of comic qualification — the word 'possibly' implies genuine uncertainty about whether hitting his mother with a car was intentional, which is deeply dark. The deadpan delivery (it's listed alongside other sins without emphasis) is perfect. Three words do extraordinary work. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I almost let him choke to death right there on the football field. / I looked the other way when my wig-based parent company turned a bunch of children orange.
jokes.setup: Jack continues his confession, listing sins.
jokes.punchline: 'Wig-based parent company turned a bunch of children orange' — the specific absurdity of a wig company that also turns children orange, delivered as corporate negligence on par with letting someone choke.
jokes.explanation: The 'wig-based parent company' is a great absurdist corporate detail — it implies a conglomerate whose primary business is wigs but which apparently also has a children's product division with serious safety issues. The specificity of 'orange' is the right choice. Part of the escalating confession list.

jokes.text: I once claimed I am God during a deposition.
jokes.setup: Jack continues listing his sins.
jokes.punchline: Claiming to be God during a legal deposition — a setting where such a claim has maximal legal and social consequences — is a perfect Jack sin: grandiose, legally reckless, and entirely believable.
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The setting (a deposition) is the key — claiming to be God in casual conversation is just eccentric, but in a legal deposition it's both potentially perjurous and reveals the depth of Jack's narcissism. 'I once claimed I am God during a deposition' is a complete story in eleven words. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: And... I may have sodomized our former Vice President while under the influence of some weapons-grade narcotics. / It feels good to say that out loud, actually. / That one was weighing on me.
jokes.setup: Jack has been escalating through increasingly serious sins.
jokes.punchline: The confession peaks with a Vice Presidential sodomy incident under 'weapons-grade narcotics,' followed by the relieved postscript 'It feels good to say that out loud, actually. That one was weighing on me.' — the therapeutic framing of a completely unconscionable act.
jokes.explanation: The escalation climax of the confession sequence. 'Weapons-grade narcotics' is an inspired specific modifier. The real joke is the follow-up: the relief of confession is a Catholic concept applied to something so extreme that the priest's silence becomes its own joke. 'That one was weighing on me' as a confession-relief punchline is perfect. Part of the same escalating confession sequence as jokes 46-48.

jokes.text: Then what brought you here tonight? / What brought me here? What brings anyone anywhere? Why do men build bridges? Why are there jets? / I was hoping to have sex tonight.
jokes.setup: The priest asks why Jack came to church if not to confess. Jack builds to a philosophical crescendo ('Why do men build bridges? Why are there jets?').
jokes.punchline: The philosophical buildup deflates completely into the mundane: 'I was hoping to have sex tonight.' The contrast between the rhetorical grandeur and the simple, selfish answer is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection structure — philosophical inflation followed by bathetic deflation. 'Why do men build bridges? Why are there jets?' sets up a profound answer. 'I was hoping to have sex tonight' is the anti-climax. The structure is very clean and the punchline is perfectly specific. Jack's complete lack of shame makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Have you ever made love to a woman, Father? / Come on, man. / Imagine cradling your face into the curve of a velvety-soft neck / your hands cupping the warm heft of the greatest pair of... / I need backup! Harvard did not prepare me for this.
jokes.setup: Jack begins a rhapsodic, inappropriate description of Elisa's physical attributes to a priest in a confession booth.
jokes.punchline: The priest breaks and calls for backup — 'Harvard did not prepare me for this' — which is both a callback to the Harvard/Princeton exchange and a perfect characterization of Jack's power to overwhelm even trained religious counselors.
jokes.explanation: 'Harvard did not prepare me for this' is an excellent callback to the Ivy League credential competition — now Harvard's education is explicitly insufficient against Jack's rhetorical sexuality. The cringe comedy of Jack describing a woman's body to a celibate priest in confession is well-executed, and the priest's panicked breakdown is the right reaction.

jokes.text: I like your bracelets. Girls in my school get them for doing different things on the bus. Blue is for showing your boobs. Purple is for doing stuff over your clothes. Black is for doing stuff...
jokes.setup: Bethany is meeting Liz for the first time and appears to be making innocent conversation.
jokes.punchline: The bracelet code she describes is a sex-act coding system among schoolchildren — delivered with complete casualness by a child, which makes it maximally uncomfortable and funny.
jokes.explanation: Dark and effective. The bracelet sex code was a real mid-2000s moral panic, which grounds the absurdity in cultural truth. Bethany's casual, informative delivery (she's just sharing knowledge) makes it cringe-funny. The escalating list of colors and acts, cut off before 'black' is defined, is the right structural choice — leave it to the imagination.

jokes.text: Whoa. Wow, Liz, did you kill the whole bottle?
jokes.setup: Drew returns from talking to his ex-wife outside. Liz is apparently visibly drunk.
jokes.punchline: Drew's shocked reaction implies Liz has consumed an entire bottle of wine in the short time he was outside — a visual gag we see through his reaction.
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat — Liz stress-drinking the entire bottle in Drew's absence is consistent with her character and the disaster of the date. Not particularly original but lands well as a beat.

jokes.text: That's my aunt. She is not going to like you.
jokes.setup: Liz hears the name 'Gloria' on Drew's phone and wonders how many ex-wives he has.
jokes.punchline: Bethany coolly informs Liz it's an aunt — then adds 'She is not going to like you' as a matter-of-fact observation, delivered with the deadpan of a child who has seen this pattern before.
jokes.explanation: Bethany's deadpan assessments of adult situations are consistently funny. 'She is not going to like you' as a casual forecast delivered by a child is dark and funny — it implies she's seen her father's dates come and go and knows the family's verdict in advance.

jokes.text: Not just any entertainment — the best singer in the world... Michael McDonald.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has arranged entertainment for Jennifer at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: He builds up 'the best singer in the world' and reveals: Michael McDonald — a sincere choice that's funny because of the gap between 'best singer in the world' and the specific reality of Michael McDonald (a beloved but distinctly non-glamorous yacht-rock singer).
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between the superlative ('best singer in the world') and Michael McDonald, whose musical identity is very specific and not what the setup implies. Kenneth's complete sincerity is essential — he genuinely believes this. Works as character comedy for Kenneth (who has specific, earnest tastes).

jokes.text: Wow, he does not sound good live.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has arranged Michael McDonald to perform live.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's immediate honest assessment — 'he does not sound good live' — delivered after introducing him as 'the best singer in the world,' is a perfect deflation.
jokes.explanation: The immediate callback undercuts the buildup beautifully. Kenneth's candid 'he does not sound good live' after his elaborate superlative introduction is excellent deadpan understatement. The brevity is the strength.

jokes.text: You tortured that poor priest. / You want an intellectual argument? Fine. But I should warn you I went to Princeton. [callback to earlier confession scene]
jokes.setup: Elisa confronts Jack about his behavior in the confession booth.
jokes.punchline: Elisa's 'you tortured that poor priest' frames Jack's confession as torture — which is accurate given what we heard — and the line lands as an understatement of what was a very extreme scene.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback line — it acknowledges the confession scene's extremity with understatement. Not particularly strong as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: No. / But I saw your photo with the Pope. / That's just good business. I have photos with a lot of people — The Dalai Lama, Rabbi Yossef, Toby Keith...
jokes.setup: Elisa confronts Jack about whether he believes in the Catholic Church. He says no.
jokes.punchline: His photo with the Pope is 'just good business' — the Pontiff is a networking contact. The list of spiritual leaders culminating in Toby Keith is the joke — Toby Keith as a spiritual authority figure equivalent to the Dalai Lama is absurd and perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent list joke — 'The Dalai Lama, Rabbi Yossef, Toby Keith' escalates from credible religious leaders to a country music star as if they occupy equivalent spiritual/business prestige. 'Just good business' as a framing for the Pope relationship is perfect Jack. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: You know what your problem is, Jack? You intellectualize everything with your big head. / Well, you have big boobs. / Which you will never touch again! / This conversation has taken an unfortunate turn.
jokes.setup: Elisa criticizes Jack for intellectualizing everything 'with your big head.'
jokes.punchline: Jack retorts with 'Well, you have big boobs' — a complete non-sequitur as a counter-argument — Elisa escalates to 'Which you will never touch again!' — and Jack closes with 'This conversation has taken an unfortunate turn.' The formal register of the closing line against the content of the argument is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Very funny escalating exchange. 'Well, you have big boobs' as a debate response is childish and Jack knows it — which is why his closing 'This conversation has taken an unfortunate turn' is so funny: he's suddenly adopting corporate formality to describe the disaster his own non-sequitur created. The structure of setup (intellectual critique), counter (physical non-sequitur), consequence (threat), and formal assessment of the situation is tight and escalates well. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: How dare you say something like that so close to the statue of Santa Lucia... the patron saint of judgmental statues.
jokes.setup: Jack says something inappropriate near a church statue.
jokes.punchline: Santa Lucia is a real saint, but 'patron saint of judgmental statues' is a made-up characterization that implies statues have feelings and specifically judgmental ones — delivered with complete sincerity by Elisa.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best absurdist jokes. 'The patron saint of judgmental statues' is a perfect 30 Rock invention — it sounds like a real Catholic thing (saints do have specific domains) but is completely invented. The specificity of 'judgmental' is the key word. Elisa's sincere delivery of this absurd concept is essential.

jokes.text: Go to your stupid restaurant. Eat your gold ice cream. / Please come with me. / No. You blew it, Jack. And now, you will never see the crazy underwears I have on.
jokes.setup: Elisa is ending the fight by dismissing Jack.
jokes.punchline: 'You will never see the crazy underwears I have on' — the plural 'underwears,' the modifier 'crazy,' and the timing (announcing the loss as punishment) is funny because it simultaneously reveals something intriguing and slams the door on it.
jokes.explanation: The plural 'underwears' (Elisa's ESL English) is perfect — it's funnier than 'underwear' would be. 'Crazy underwears' as a parting threat/announcement is a great line. Jack's reaction ('What kind of God would let that happen?') is the cherry on top.

jokes.text: Elisa! / What kind of God would let that happen?
jokes.setup: Elisa has left. Jack calls after her, then addresses the heavens.
jokes.punchline: Jack rephrases a classic theodicy question ('What kind of God would allow suffering?') but applies it to missing out on Elisa's underwear — treating his romantic/sexual disappointment as a theological crisis.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful quick joke — Jack channels the 'problem of evil' theological argument but about not seeing underwear. 'What kind of God would let that happen?' is both a parody of his earlier anti-faith position and a genuine expression of his priorities. One of the episode's most quotable lines. The economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm sorry... is this, like, a 'Sixth Sense' thing? Should I bring a place setting for your friend?
jokes.setup: Drew's mother is apparently speaking to someone invisible/imaginary in her hospital room.
jokes.punchline: A hospital staff member asks if this is a 'Sixth Sense' thing — referencing the film's invisible-dead-person conceit — and offers to bring a place setting for the nonexistent friend, treating a potentially supernatural situation with bureaucratic hospitality.
jokes.explanation: A funny, slightly dark joke that treats a potentially delusional elderly woman with cheerful pragmatism. The 'Sixth Sense' reference works because it's specific and the logical extension (place setting for a ghost) is the right absurdist move.

jokes.text: The woman he thinks is his sister is really his mother. / What? / I'm his grandmother.
jokes.setup: Drew's mother is asking 'Mandy' (actually Liz) to deliver a message — that there's a secret about Drew's family.
jokes.punchline: The secret escalates: his 'sister' is actually his mother — then immediately topped: the person telling Liz this is actually his grandmother. A compressed revelation that each layer adds a generation of deception.
jokes.explanation: Masterfully compressed family secret escalation. The two-step reveal — his sister is his mother / I'm his grandmother — packs an enormous amount of dark soap-opera revelation into very few words. The structure is perfect: first revelation creates shock, second revelation recontextualizes everything. The economy (nine words for the second revelation) is exceptional. One of the episode's best structural jokes.

jokes.text: You have to tell him or I won't get into Heaven.
jokes.setup: Drew's grandmother is pressing Liz to deliver the family secret message.
jokes.punchline: Her motivation is purely transactional — tell Drew this devastating truth, or she won't get into Heaven. Using Heaven admission as leverage for a secret that will devastate her grandson is darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: The transactional framing of heavenly admission as the motivation for truth-telling is funny — it makes faith mercenary in the same way Jack makes everything mercenary. Good dark comedy.

jokes.text: Thank you for a truly unbelievable evening.
jokes.setup: After the deathbed family secret revelation, Liz processes the entire night.
jokes.punchline: Her summary — 'a truly unbelievable evening' — is the master understatement for a date that included toilet exposure, a wardrobe malfunction, a pyro child, a bitter ex-wife, and a dying grandmother with a secret family tree.
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical beat that serves as a structural pause after the escalation of the evening. The understatement works because the audience has witnessed everything — 'unbelievable' is doing maximum work here.

jokes.text: It doesn't have to end here, y'allsies.
jokes.setup: A scene is apparently wrapping up.
jokes.punchline: 'Y'allsies' — Kenneth's folksy plural 'y'all' made even more diminutive with an '-sies' suffix — is pure Kenneth invented vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: Another Kenneth invented folksy term. 'Y'allsies' is endearing and surprising enough to earn a laugh. Pure character comedy.

jokes.text: Wait, this isn't right. / Kenneth, why do you suddenly sound white? / I lied to you, Jennifer. I was too scared to talk to you so my sophisticated friend, Tracy said the things that I couldn't.
jokes.setup: Jennifer notices Kenneth's voice has changed — presumably Tracy (who was voicing him) has been replaced by Kenneth's actual voice.
jokes.punchline: 'Why do you suddenly sound white?' — Jennifer's assessment of Kenneth's vocal racial presentation — and the reveal that Tracy (a Black man) was doing Kenneth's voice for the date is a deeply layered racial/class joke delivered with complete absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Complex joke — Jennifer, who is blind, has been hearing 'Tracy's voice' as Kenneth's, and now Kenneth's actual voice sounds different enough that she notices a racial shift. 'My sophisticated friend Tracy' as a description of Tracy Jordan is its own joke. The situation is absurd but the joke works on multiple levels simultaneously.

jokes.text: That you're the sweetest... prettiest, blindest girl I've ever met. And when I'm with you, my heart jumps like a frog on July asphalt right before it dies.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is finally speaking for himself to Jennifer, telling her what he would have said.
jokes.punchline: His romantic declaration culminates in 'my heart jumps like a frog on July asphalt right before it dies' — a folksy simile that begins as sweet and ends in a frog's death as the image for love.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a peak Kenneth Parcell moment. 'Like a frog on July asphalt right before it dies' is a genuinely inspired simile — it starts as a standard jumping-heart metaphor and the specificity of 'July asphalt right before it dies' transforms it into something darkly precise and completely unique to Kenneth. The bathos of ending a sincere love declaration with a dying frog image is perfectly crafted. Highly quotable, maximum character integration.

jokes.text: Can I feel your face? / Yeah. [Kenneth's reaction beat — presumably uncomfortable/delighted]
jokes.setup: Jennifer has been moved by Kenneth's declaration and wants to 'see' his face.
jokes.punchline: The touching-face moment, while genuine, becomes a comedic reaction beat as Kenneth experiences an intimate moment that is presumably weird and sweet simultaneously — the awkward pause and implied physical comedy is the joke.
jokes.explanation: More sentimental than comedic, but the extended beat of face-touching creates mild awkward comedy. Works as a visual gag we infer from context.

jokes.text: Oh, look at the time. I forgot I have a... a thing.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has just had what seemed like a romantic moment — Jennifer touching his face.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's sudden exit — the most transparent possible excuse ('I forgot I have a... a thing') — immediately after the intimate moment reveals that feeling Kenneth's face has repelled rather than attracted her.
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of the romantic arc. The pause before 'a thing' is itself the punchline — she literally felt his face and immediately needed to leave. The structure is clean and the deflation of the romantic buildup is earned. 'A thing' as the excuse is maximally vague and therefore maximally funny.

jokes.text: That is cold, blind lady! / Oh, and by the way... you are not so attractive, yourself. / No, I'm... I'm pretty sure I'm hot. / Yes, you are. I tried.
jokes.setup: Jennifer has abruptly left. Tracy confronts her.
jokes.punchline: Jennifer's parting shot — 'you are not so attractive, yourself' — to Tracy, who the show frames as conventionally handsome/famous. Tracy's response 'I'm pretty sure I'm hot' and Jennifer's 'Yes, you are. I tried.' — confirming she knew he was attractive but tried to insult him anyway — is the final beat.
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing beat for the Jennifer/Kenneth storyline. 'Yes, you are. I tried.' is a perfect closing line — Jennifer acknowledges she KNEW Tracy was attractive and attempted an insult anyway out of spite. The honesty of the admission makes it funnier. Well-structured two-step exchange.

jokes.text: Let's do this again sometime... except have it not be anything like this at all.
jokes.setup: Drew is closing out the disastrous first date with Liz.
jokes.punchline: The standard 'let's do this again' is immediately qualified with 'except have it not be anything like this at all' — a polite framing of a complete disaster.
jokes.explanation: Clean and economical joke on a cliché — 'let's do this again' is immediately destroyed by the qualifier. The structure of setup (cliché) followed by immediate inversion works well.

jokes.text: Uh... Liz? You know, my mom did just die. / Funny story. Hear me out. / I'll have a, uh... ...a McFlurry, please.
jokes.setup: Drew's mother has just died. He reminds Liz of this, seemingly for comfort. Liz starts to tell a 'funny story.'
jokes.punchline: We expect an awkward, inappropriate funny story. Instead, we cut to Liz ordering a McFlurry — revealing she's taken Drew to McDonald's immediately after his mother's death, and the 'funny story' is presumably how that happened.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes and a perfect callback to the McFlurry motif. The gap between 'my mom just died' and the McFlurry destination is the entire joke — Liz's response to grief is McDonald's, and 'Funny story. Hear me out.' as a preamble to this revelation is perfect. The 'Funny story' delay before the cut to McDonald's is expertly structured. High originality, economy, character integration.

jokes.text: And I have a coupon. You know where I found it? In the collection plate. It was a sign.
jokes.setup: Jack is also at McDonald's. He has a coupon.
jokes.punchline: He found the coupon in the church collection plate — and treats it as a divine sign that brought him to McDonald's. The collection plate (where money goes to God) yielding a McDonald's coupon is a perfect inversion, and Jack genuinely reading it as a sign is great character comedy.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful convergence of the episode's themes — faith, capitalism, and McDonald's. Finding a McDonald's coupon in a church collection plate and reading it as a sign from God is a perfect synthesis of Jack's faith-in-capitalism and the episode's religion theme. The structure (where did you find it? / collection plate) works as a clean setup/punchline. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Someone's trying to tell us that we belong together. Maybe it's God. Maybe it's Ray Kroc. Maybe it's the Hamburgler.
jokes.setup: Jack and Elisa are reconciling at McDonald's. Jack muses on who brought them together.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list — God, Ray Kroc (McDonald's founder), the Hamburgler — treats these three as equivalent cosmic forces, with the Hamburgler as the absurdist peak.
jokes.explanation: Perfect list escalation. God → Ray Kroc → the Hamburgler is a brilliant comedic ladder — each step makes sense in the McDonald's context but the Hamburgler as a deity figure is the absurdist peak. 'Maybe it's the Hamburgler' as the closing cosmic force is both unexpected and completely logical given the setting. Highly quotable, great economy.

jokes.text: Boy, I hope that guy's not planning to kill and eat her.
jokes.setup: Jack and Elisa apparently witness a couple with an ambiguous dynamic nearby.
jokes.punchline: Jack's casual observation — 'I hope that guy's not planning to kill and eat her' — treats cannibalistic murder as a reasonable thing to worry about in a McDonald's on Valentine's night, delivered as a mild concern rather than alarm.
jokes.explanation: Dark, economical, and very funny. Jack's delivery as a mild concern ('I hope...') about potential cannibalism is the joke — the same register one might use to say 'I hope they have the fish sandwich.' Well-crafted closing dark joke.

jokes.text: Jack, you're such a romantic.
jokes.setup: Jack has just expressed concern that a nearby man might murder and eat a woman.
jokes.punchline: Elisa responds with 'Jack, you're such a romantic' — treating his cannibalism concern as evidence of romantic sensitivity. The irony is total and the deadpan delivery closes the episode on a perfect note.
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing line. 'Jack, you're such a romantic' applied to a cannibalism remark is a masterclass in ironic understatement as an episode closer. The economy (five words) and the total inversion (murder concern = romantic) is executed perfectly. Works as both a callback and a standalone closer.

tmdb_overview: Liz insists that she and Drew have their first official date on Valentine's Day. Elisa brings Jack to church to celebrate the day, which is very different from the way he traditionally celebrates. Kenneth employs the help of Tracy to try to win the affection of a new worker.
insight: Valentine's episode sustains 82-point pace with 48 jokes across character comedy and wordplay.
